client: I've been having a really hard time with something that probably sounds kind of silly, but it's been affecting my daily routine more than I expected. There's this café near my work that I used to go to all the time with my ex, and now every single time I walk in there, my heart just starts racing and I feel completely overwhelmed, like I need to get out immediately. I'm not even sure therapy can really fix something like this — it feels almost too specific, too tied to a place, you know?
therapist: What you're describing doesn't sound silly at all — your nervous system has connected that café to something that mattered deeply to you, and that kind of emotional memory is incredibly real and valid. The racing heart and urge to escape are actually your body trying to protect you, even if it feels overwhelming in the moment. And I want you to know that what you're experiencing is exactly the kind of thing therapy can help with — we can work together to gently shift your relationship with those memories so they don't have to hold so much power over your daily life.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, and it does help a little to hear it framed that way — like my body is trying to protect me rather than just freaking out for no reason. But I guess I'm still skeptical about the "shifting my relationship with memories" part, because I've tried just telling myself it's fine and it's just a place, and that doesn't work at all. It feels like the anxiety just kind of overrides whatever rational thing I'm trying to tell myself.
therapist: You've actually just identified something really important — trying to logic your way out of anxiety rarely works, because the part of your brain triggering that fear response isn't listening to rational thoughts in those moments. What we'd be doing in CBT is less about telling yourself "it's fine" and more about gradually teaching your nervous system through *experience* that the café is safe, so your body starts to believe it too. It's a bit like the difference between reading about swimming and actually getting in the water — does that distinction feel like it might make sense for what you've been going through?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, that distinction actually does make some sense to me — like I can intellectually understand the café is just a building, but my body clearly hasn't gotten that memo. But when you say "gradually teaching my nervous system through experience," I'm already feeling a bit nervous about what that means in practice, because if it involves actually going back in there on purpose, I'm not sure I'm ready for that. The last time I walked in, I lasted maybe two minutes before I had to leave, and it was honestly embarrassing.
therapist: The embarrassment you felt in that moment makes complete sense, but I want to gently challenge the idea that leaving was a failure — your body was doing exactly what it's been trained to do, and that took courage just to walk in at all. The good news is that "gradually" really does mean gradually — we'd never start by throwing you back into the deep end, and you'd always be in control of the pace. Can I ask, when you imagine approaching this in very small steps, what feels like it might be the tiniest, most manageable version of that for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Hmm, when I really think about it, maybe the smallest step would be something like... just walking past the café without going in, like on the other side of the street? But even as I say that, I'm second-guessing myself, because what if even seeing it from a distance triggers that same panic response and then I've just made things worse by exposing myself to it. I guess I'm worried that doing it wrong could somehow reinforce the anxiety rather than help it.
therapist: Walking past on the other side of the street is actually a really thoughtful first step, and it shows good instincts about your own limits. Your concern about "doing it wrong" is understandable, but here's something reassuring — briefly seeing the café from a distance, even if it stirs something, won't reinforce the anxiety the way you're imagining, as long as you're not fleeing in a panic; just noticing a feeling and continuing to walk is actually a small win in itself. What do you think it would feel like to try that, knowing that whatever you feel in that moment is just information, not a setback?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think it might feel... manageable, maybe, if I really focus on the idea that whatever I feel is just information. But I'm also realizing that I'd probably avoid that street entirely on a bad day, like if I'm already stressed from work or feeling low, and then I'd feel guilty about avoiding it, which kind of adds another layer on top of everything. Is it okay to only try it on days when I feel somewhat stable, or does that become its own kind of avoidance?
therapist: That's such a thoughtful question, and the fact that you're already anticipating the guilt trap shows real self-awareness. Starting on more stable days is actually a smart, compassionate strategy — not avoidance — because you're building a foundation of success your nervous system can learn from, rather than setting yourself up to be overwhelmed. The goal is to gradually expand what "stable enough" looks like over time, so the window of days when you feel ready slowly gets wider.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That actually makes me feel a bit relieved, because I think I've been treating every moment of avoidance like a moral failure, and hearing that being strategic about timing isn't the same as giving up is genuinely helpful. But I'm also wondering — what do I do about the guilt on the days I do avoid it, because that feeling doesn't just go away on its own, and sometimes it kind of snowballs into me feeling bad about myself in a more general way. It's like the café thing becomes this symbol of everything I can't handle.
therapist: The way the café has become a symbol for "everything I can't handle" is such an important thing to name, because that's where the guilt really gets its power — it's no longer just about a building, it's become evidence for a story you're telling yourself about who you are. On the days you avoid it, it might help to gently ask yourself: "Is avoiding this street today actually proof I can't handle things, or is it just one decision I made on one hard day?" That small shift — from self-judgment to curiosity — is something we can really build on together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of asking myself that question, but I'm honestly not sure I'll remember to do it in the moment when the guilt is already spiraling — it's like when I'm in that headspace, I'm not thinking clearly enough to pause and reframe anything. And there's also a part of me that worries if I let myself off the hook too easily, I'll just keep avoiding indefinitely and never actually make progress. How do I find the balance between being compassionate with myself and still holding myself accountable?
therapist: The balance you're looking for actually lives in something concrete — rather than relying on remembering to reframe in a spiral, we could work on creating a simple, specific plan ahead of time, like a brief note on your phone that's already written for those moments, so your calmer self can speak to your harder moments. Self-compassion and accountability aren't opposites here — the accountability piece is actually showing up in the planning and the small steps, not in punishing yourself on the days it doesn't go perfectly. What do you think it would feel like to have something like that already waiting for you, rather than having to find the words yourself when you're struggling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, having something already written does sound more realistic than expecting myself to think clearly mid-spiral, and I can see why that might actually work. But I'm a little worried about what I'd even write — like, I don't want it to sound so generic that I just roll my eyes at it when I'm feeling bad, because I've seen those kinds of affirmations before and they just feel hollow to me in the moment. How do I make sure it actually feels like something I'd believe rather than just a platitude I wrote when I was feeling okay?
therapist: You're absolutely right to be skeptical of hollow affirmations — the most effective version of this isn't something inspirational you found online, it's something specific to *you*, written in your own voice, that references your actual experience. Think about what your most compassionate friend would say to you about the café specifically, or even what you'd say to someone you care about who was in your exact situation — that's usually much closer to something you'll actually believe. Would it feel okay to try drafting just one sentence like that together, something that feels honest rather than polished?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I think I could try that... maybe something like "Avoiding the café today doesn't mean you're broken, it just means today was hard and that's allowed." But even as I say it out loud, I notice I feel a little uncomfortable, like I'm not sure I fully believe it yet, and part of me wonders if writing it down will feel self-indulgent or dramatic. I guess I'm also realizing that I don't really have a compassionate friend I'd talk to about this — it's actually kind of lonely carrying this around by myself.
therapist: That sentence you just wrote is genuinely good — it's specific, it's honest, and the fact that it makes you a little uncomfortable probably means it's touching something real rather than skating over it. I also want to stay with what you just shared at the end, because saying "I'm carrying this alone" took courage, and that loneliness sounds like it might be one of the heavier parts of all this. How long have you been holding this without someone to share it with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, probably since the breakup, which was about eight months ago now, and I think I've been telling myself I should be over it by now so I haven't really let myself talk about it with anyone. My friends knew my ex too, so it felt complicated and awkward to bring it up, and after a while it just felt like too much time had passed to suddenly start talking about it. So I've just been kind of quietly managing it on my own, which I guess hasn't been working as well as I thought.
therapist: Eight months of quietly carrying this, while also telling yourself you should already be done with it — that's an incredibly heavy thing to have been managing alone, and it makes complete sense that it hasn't been working, because we genuinely aren't built to process loss in isolation. I notice there's something in the way you're describing all of this that sounds almost matter-of-fact, like you're reporting it from a distance, and I'm wondering if part of you has gotten so used to holding it together that it's hard to fully let yourself feel the weight of it. What would it mean for you to finally not have to manage this alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
